content: Health science is a branch of applied science that focuses on health and encompasses numerous subfields. It involves two primary approaches: first, the study and research of the human body and health-related issues to understand how humans and animals function; and second, the application of this knowledge to improve health, prevent diseases, and develop treatments. Research in health science is built upon foundational sciences such as biology, chemistry, and physics, as well as interdisciplinary fields like medical sociology. Key research-oriented disciplines contributing significantly to health science include biochemistry, epidemiology, and genetics. Applied health sciences aim not only to understand health but also to directly enhance the health of individuals and populations. Fields such as biomedical engineering, biotechnology, nursing, nutrition, pharmacology, public health, psychology, physical therapy, and medicine are examples of applied health sciences. The delivery of services to improve health is referred to as health care, which is a major component of the health sciences industry—a multi-billion-dollar sector that intersects with life sciences, health care, and medical diagnostics. Medical research, both basic and applied, is conducted to evaluate the safety and efficacy of new treatments through clinical trials or to develop new therapies in preclinical research. Advances in medical research have significantly contributed to the increased human lifespan over the past century. The Human Genome Project has paved the way for new diagnostic tools and treatments, although challenges such as antibiotic resistance and the obesity epidemic persist. Health care involves the prevention, treatment, and management of illnesses, as well as the preservation of mental and physical well-being. According to the World Health Organization, health care encompasses all goods and services designed to promote health, including preventive, curative, and palliative interventions for individuals and populations. Health care systems may be organized at the governmental level, such as the National Health Service in the UK, or through collaborative efforts like Shared Care. The field of health care includes a wide range of professions, with medicine and biomedicine being the dominant conventional practices in the Western world. Common areas of health care include medicine, nursing, midwifery, and various forms of therapy, such as physical, occupational, speech, and respiratory therapy. Public health focuses on the impact of environmental factors and health care resources on population health, often targeting specific groups like mothers and children. Dietitians specialize in educating individuals about proper nutrition, particularly for those with specific dietary needs, such as people with diabetes or celiac disease. Other areas of health care include first aid, triage, dental health, counseling, hospice care, home care, alternative medicine, pharmacology, and toxicology. Veterinary medicine is a distinct branch of health science dedicated to animal health, including disease prevention, treatment, and food safety. Conventional Western health practices include fields such as allopathic medicine, athletic training, dentistry, dietetics, epidemiology, genetic counseling, medical physics, nursing, nutrition, occupational therapy, optometry, pharmacology, physical therapy, psychology, public health, speech-language pathology, surgery, and veterinary medicine. Complementary and alternative medicine encompasses practices like chiropractic care, herbalism, homeopathy, naturopathy, and osteopathy (outside the U.S.). Spiritually-based healing methods include faith healing, Reiki, and shamanism. Traditional medicine includes systems like Ayurveda, traditional Chinese medicine, and Native American healing practices. Historical health practices of interest include bloodletting, medieval medicine, and trepanation. Health science frequently intersects with medical ethics, which addresses complex issues such as patient privacy, euthanasia, abortion, human cloning, stem cell research, and genetic engineering. These topics are often controversial and require careful ethical consideration. The origins of health science date back to the earliest human civilizations, as humans have always sought solutions for illness, injury, and health-related challenges like childbirth. With advancements in technology and the integration of pure sciences, the accuracy and efficacy of health sciences have significantly improved. However, many cultures continue to use traditional remedies, including herbs and culturally specific practices, some of which lack scientific validation.
